title: COVID-19 in Brazil: An Analysis About the Consumption of Information on Social Networks
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 97 most-engaging Portuguese-language COVID-19 links circulating on Brazilian social networks (Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Pinterest) in March 2020, retrieved via BuzzSumo. The authors fact-checked each link against scientific papers, official sources and other journalism using the Wardle & Derakhshan typology and report that mis/disinformation accounted for 13.5% of the analysed links, broken down into false connection 5.2%, misleading content 4.1% and fabricated content 4.1%. That is a share of items classified false/misleading with a stated denominator, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.platform: Facebook, Twitter, Reddit and Pinterest (engagement aggregated by BuzzSumo)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-engaging Portuguese-language COVID-19 links in Brazil classified as mis/disinformation
estimates.value_raw: 13.5% of the analysed links, classified as false connection (5.2%), misleading content (4.1%) and fabricated content (4.1%); verified 82.4%, non-verifiable 4.1%; n = 97 links
estimates.denominator: 97 Portuguese-language links about COVID-19 with the highest total engagement (Facebook shares/comments/likes/reactions + Twitter shares + Reddit shares/comments + Pinterest shares) between 1 and 31 March 2020, retrieved with BuzzSumo's free tier for the keywords 'COVID-19' and 'coronavirus' (100 links collected, minus 1 published in Portugal and 2 duplicates)
estimates.definition: A link counted as mis/disinformation if the authors' qualitative fact-check placed it in one of the Wardle & Derakhshan categories other than 'verified content' or 'non-verifiable content' - here false connection (headline/visuals contradict the body), misleading content (framing by selective or omitted data) or fabricated content (100% false, created to deceive). Manipulated content, false context and parody/satire were available categories but none were found.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation indicates distorted, ambiguous or unclarified information from misinterpretation or false connections. Disinformation, on the other hand, refers to intentionally false information, including content out of context, impostor content (falsely attributed to the news media or a personality), manipulated content (genuine information, such as photos and videos, edited to deceive) or completely fabricated content."
estimates.source_quote: In terms of ‘accuracy’, there was a predominance of links with verified information about COVID-19 (82.4%). On the other hand, ‘mis/disinformation’ accounted for 13.5% of the analysed links, classified as false connection (5.2%), misleading content (4.1%) and fabricated content (4.1%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. JCOM 19(07)(2020)A07 9; Figure 1; repeated in the Abstract and in Final considerations
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The three authors applied the fact-checking method qualitatively, comparing each link's content with scientific papers, official sources and other journalistic articles, and classified it with the Wardle & Derakhshan (2017) typology plus an added 'non-verifiable content' category for opinions and polls. No coder count per item, no double-coding and no inter-rater reliability statistic are reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: From BuzzSumo, we collected 100 topics with the keywords 'COVID-19' and 'coronavirus' that generated the highest engagement on Facebook, Twitter, Reddit and Pinterest between the 1st and the 31st of March, 2020. ... We used the Portuguese language as a filter. Among the one hundred links collected, 99 were published by Brazilian websites and only one from Portugal, which was therefore excluded from our sample. After excluding this link and two others that were repeated, the final sample consisted of 97 links.
estimates.notes: CONSTRUCT JUDGEMENT for the adjudicator: coded CONTENT because the denominator is a set of 97 items and each item counts once, regardless of its engagement; the alternative reading is SHARING with sharing_subtype=content_share, since the items were SELECTED by engagement rank. I followed the rule that top-N / most-viewed rank-truncated sets stay in the topic's scope with denom_selection=curated. This is emphatically not an engagement-weighted share: the paper reports that mis/disinformation links averaged MORE engagement than verified ones, so an engagement-weighted share would be higher than 13.5% (a weighted figure is nowhere stated and I did not compute one). Raw counts are never printed; the stated percentages imply 5 + 4 + 4 = 13 of 97 links (13.4%), consistent with the reported 13.5% to within rounding, and with 80 verified (82.4%) + 13 + 4 non-verifiable (4.1%) = 97. Sample size is capped at 100 links purely by BuzzSumo's free tier, which the authors state explicitly.

estimates.definition: A link counted only if classified 'fabricated content' - 'Content that is 100% false, created to deceive or harm' (Table 1) - excluding misleading content and false connection
estimates.misinfo_def: "Fabricated content: Content that is 100% false, created to deceive or harm" (Table 1, after Wardle and Derakhshan 2017)
estimates.source_quote: ‘mis/disinformation’ accounted for 13.5% of the analysed links, classified as false connection (5.2%), misleading content (4.1%) and fabricated content (4.1%).

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors' qualitative fact-check against scientific papers, official sources and other journalism; Wardle & Derakhshan typology; no inter-rater reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In step 1, we applied the 'fact-checking' method qualitatively to classify the content found according to its 'accuracy'. The accuracy of these contents was determined by comparing it with information from scientific papers, official sources and other journalistic articles.
estimates.notes: Kept as the strict-definition variant of the 13.5% row (same country x platform x measure cell), because the review codes breadth as a moderator and this is the paper's only outright-fabrication figure: 4.1% versus 13.5% shows exactly how much the broad definition adds. The remaining two subcategories (false connection 5.2%, misleading content 4.1%) are not extracted as separate rows - they are neither the headline nor a nested definition, and their sum with fabricated is already captured by the 13.5% row.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (a) SOURCE CONCENTRATION, flagged for the adjudicator - 'almost half (48.5%) of the most engaging content was produced by only four journalistic outlets ... UOL ... R7 ... G1 and O Globo', out of 45 websites identified. This is formally a top-group-to-share statement (4/45 = 8.9% of sources accounting for 48.5% of the items) and could be built into a CONCENTRATION row, but the concentrated group is mainstream journalism, not misinformation, and the 48.5% is a share of ITEMS in a rank-truncated set rather than of exposure or of sharing, so neither conc_dimension value fits. I left it out to avoid entering an all-content source concentration into a misinformation-concentration analysis; the numbers are here should the review want it. (b) Website type: 45 websites of which 35 'professional' (77.8%) and 10 (22.2%) 'non-professional', and within professional 30 journalistic (85.7%). The professional/non-professional criteria are transparency criteria (stated editorial policy, physical address, named editorial team, sources cited), so a wholly accurate site can be 'non-professional' and a wholly false one 'professional' - this measures outlet transparency, not information quality on a validated instrument, so I did not force it into QUALITY. (c) Engagement means (total 540,447; verified 534,524; mis/disinformation 620,800; non-verifiable 456,275) - means, not shares; and an engagement-weighted misinformation share would require me to multiply and sum across categories, which R8 forbids. NOTE an internal inconsistency here: the Results text says mis/disinformation content had '602,800 interactions' while Table 3 says 620,800. (d) Total engagement figures (52,455,137 interactions; Facebook 52,247,900; Twitter 201,108; Reddit 6,100; Pinterest 29) - volume denominators, no misinformation numerator attached. (e) 'Verified information (82.4%)' and 'non-verifiable content (4.1%)' - the converse and the unappraisable category. (f) Brazilian media-use statistics quoted from the Reuters Institute Digital News Report and IBGE (74% internet use; social media a news source for 67%; Facebook 54%, WhatsApp 48%, YouTube 45%, Instagram 30%, Twitter 17%) - figures cited from elsewhere, excluded per R8, and about news use rather than misinformation. (g) Findings attributed to Salaverria et al., Brennen et al. and Pulido et al. in the literature review - cited from elsewhere. (h) Table 2's caption says 'Numbers of engagement from 100 links' while the analysis is of 97 links; the engagement totals therefore appear to cover the pre-exclusion set.

rob.design: Cross-sectional quali-quantitative content analysis. Sampling frame: BuzzSumo free tier, hard-capped at 100 links, queried for 'COVID-19' and 'coronavirus' with a Portuguese-language filter, ranked by total engagement across Facebook, Twitter, Reddit and Pinterest, 1-31 March 2020; 100 links reduced to 97 after removing one Portuguese publisher and two duplicates. Coding: authors applied fact-checking qualitatively against scientific papers, official sources and other journalism, using Wardle & Derakhshan's typology plus an added 'non-verifiable' category; websites additionally classed professional/non-professional on four transparency criteria. No response rate applies. Reliability: no double-coding, no inter-rater agreement statistic, no per-item coder assignment reported - the weakest point for this estimate. Other limits the authors state: BuzzSumo cannot compare platforms (Twitter/Pinterest count only shares), bots and paid promotion are not excluded, and the sample is not a reflection of real public opinion. Engagement is overwhelmingly Facebook (52.2M of 52.5M), so the multi-platform label is nominal.
